name: Nahum

facts.author: Nahum the Elkoshite (1:1), from a town called Elkosh. Nothing more is known of him.
facts.audience: The people of Judah, who had suffered under Assyria, given as a message about Nineveh

about: About a hundred years after Jonah, Nineveh had gone back to its evil ways. Assyria had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and troubled Judah for many years. Its armies were famous for cruelty. Nahum's whole book is a burden, a heavy message, against Nineveh (1:1).

Nahum begins with the character of God. The Lord is slow to anger but great in power, and He will not let the guilty go unpunished (1:3). He is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble for those who trust in Him (1:7). For Judah, the end of Nineveh is good news of peace (1:15).

Chapters 2 and 3 describe the fall of the city in vivid pictures: chariots racing in the streets, gates opened, treasure carried away. Nineveh is no stronger than the Egyptian city of No, which had already fallen (3:8). The prophecy came true in 612 BC, when the Babylonians and the Medes destroyed Nineveh.

themes.title: God's justice
themes.text: God is patient, but He will finally judge those who do evil and refuse to turn.

themes.title: A refuge for His people
themes.text: The same God who judges Nineveh is a safe place for all who trust in Him.

themes.title: The end of the proud
themes.text: No empire is too strong for God to bring down.

themes.title: Good news of peace
themes.text: The fall of the oppressor means freedom and rest for God's people.

outline.title: The Lord is slow to anger and great in power
Nineveh will be cut off; good news for Judah
